Title: The V Is for Starting, Not for Cruising
Description: Toes out, heels in, the pizza slice shape: that is how everybody gets moving, and it is correct. It is also only for acceleration — standing starts, hills, headwind, broken tarmac. Once you are holding your speed, each skate should set down pointing straight ahead. Most skaters never make the switch and stay in the V the whole way, which gives very short glides and, at speed, becomes a sideways zigzag. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: One Drill Takes the V Out of Your Stride
Description: Push out to the side, then pause in the middle with both skates exactly parallel, close enough to squeeze an imaginary line between them. Push again, pause again. You are not training the push here — you are training the regroup, because the pushing skate has to angle out anyway. Over the weeks you shorten the pause until it vanishes and you are simply skating straight ahead. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Body Up, Knees Down — It Is Not a Squat
Description: The skating stance is not sitting back. Your shoulder stays over your hip, your chest stays upright, and it is the knees that travel forward, until the front of the kneecap covers your toes when seen from the side. Your backside finishes directly above your heels, never behind them. Four words to hold while you skate: body up, knees down. Almost everything else follows from that one shape. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Leaning Forward Puts You Where Backward Falls Start
Description: You are afraid of going down backwards, so you push your chest and head forward. It feels logical. But the body moves as one piece: that lean arrives with knees not bent enough and a backside sitting behind your heels, which drops your centre of mass into the back half of the skate — precisely where a backward fall begins. The stance you took out of fear is the one building the risk. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Practice Does Not Make Perfect, It Makes Permanent
Description: The standard advice for a flaw in your skating is to skate more. It does the opposite of what you want: whatever you repeat is what sets. Put a hundred more miles through a bad stride and you own that stride a hundred miles deeper. The way out is not volume, it is seeing what you actually do — get somebody to film you from behind and from the side, then compare it with what you believed. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: A Few Perfect Strides Beat Half an Hour of Sloppy Ones
Description: The correct skating position is a half-squat, and as a beginner you do not yet have the legs to hold it. So you tire, your knees rise, your backside drifts back, and you spend the end of the session rehearsing the exact technique you were trying to lose. That is the beginner weakness cycle. Do a few strides properly, then stop and rest — resting means standing still, not rolling badly. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: On Rough Ground, Raise Your Tempo, Do Not Push Harder
Description: Bad tarmac takes your speed away instantly, and the instinct is to push harder against it. Wrong lever. What brings the speed back is cadence: short, quick steps set down in a V, barely rolling between them, with almost no force in any single one. Picture the ground as red hot and you not wanting to leave your wheels on it. The same answer works for hills and for headwind. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Accelerate Towards the Rough Patch, Do Not Slow Into It
Description: For a short bad stretch, split your feet one in front of the other and coast across it. Shift your weight back towards midfoot and heels so your front wheels do not get tripped by the broken surface, and keep the knees soft so they soak up the bumps. The catch is that it needs speed behind it — so you build speed on the way in, which is the exact opposite of what your nerves are asking for. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Pronation Is Not a Style Problem, It Is a Joint Problem
Description: Watch a newer skater's boot roll slightly onto its inside edge with every step. It reads as a cosmetic detail and it is not one: left alone, it leads to slow-onset injuries in the ankle, knee or hip on the side that rolls. And it feeds itself, because setting the skate down in a V with the toes turned out keeps loading that same inside edge. Fix the set-down and you have started on the pronation. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: A Crossover Lands With a Bent Knee, Not a Straight One
Description: The clumpy, unstable crossover has one cause: the crossing leg arrives straight and only bends afterwards. There is a pause inside it that you can feel. The knee has to already be bent the instant the wheels touch down, front of the kneecap over the toes. Drill it on a circle — a few pushes, then cross straight into a short toe roll, back knee brushing just behind the front one. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby.
